cases.final_diagnosis: CNC-02 has a developing mechanical fault, most consistent with spindle-bearing wear (or related imbalance/loose mounting/alignment), causing recurrent vibration above the 4.50 mm/s alarm threshold. Evidence: vibration alarms at tick 914 (4.58 mm/s) and tick 919 (4.51 mm/s) (E4); readings 900-920 run about 4.15-4.58 mm/s with repeated threshold crossings (E3, E5); 20-tick trend buckets show a steady rise in mean vibration from 3.988 (840-859) to 4.317 (900-919) and max from 4.211 to 4.577 (E10); CNC-01 runs at roughly 1.8-2.2 mm/s, so the elevated level is specific to CNC-02 (E9, E11); temperature (~144-148°F, E6) and load (~53-57%, E7) are normal, ruling out overheating or overload; maintenance history shows vibration/temperature sensors checked and reading normally and spindle speed within tolerance (E12), arguing against a sensor or calibration fault. Confidence: 0.90.
Failures alternate with passes every other job, indicating a cyclic or per-job intermittent cause

CNC-05, the last machine before inspection, has an intermittent fault showing elevated vibration and axis following error, producing out-of-spec parts on some jobs and causing inspection failures on jobs 1, 2, and 4 while job 3 passed. Every job passes through CNC-05 immediately before inspection, so its intermittent defect fits the 3-of-4 failure pattern; job-specific settings (H2) are contradicted by E11, material variation (H3) by job 3 passing in the same batch, and inspection-station false rejects (H4) by the CNC-05 sensor anomalies. Confidence is about 0.80, below the 0.90 needed to intervene. Evidence that would raise it: maintenance or event records showing CNC-05 faults during jobs 1, 2, 4 but not job 3, or a direct correlation of CNC-05 vibration/following-error spikes with the failed jobs. Once confirmed, a human-approved repair on CNC-05 (repair_hydraulics, replace_bearing, or replace_servo_drive depending on the root cause) should stop the failures.

CNC-01 experienced a transient vibration disturbance, not a sustained equipment failure. Vibration spiked to 7.01-7.37 mm/s at ticks 521-524 (above the 4.50 mm/s alarm setpoint), triggering alarms at each of those ticks, then returned to baseline (~2.2 mm/s) by tick 525 and stayed there through at least tick 536. The near-zero readings (~0.08-0.20 mm/s) at ticks 537-540 indicate the machine was likely stopped or idle during that window, which does not change the alarm diagnosis. No missing samples are evident in the 519-530 window (E5 is continuous), and the abrupt spike-and-collapse pattern rules out a gradual rise or sustained trend. H1 is strongly supported; H2 (sustained mechanical problem) is contradicted by the return to baseline; H3 and H4 have no supporting evidence.

CNC-03 shows a transient vibration spike (≈5.0–5.2 mm/s, above the 4.50 threshold) at ticks 71–78, then returns to normal by ticks 79–80 (E3, E4, E5). However, during the spike the machine's load was near 0% (E6), temperature was stable (E7), no speed or setting change occurred (E9), no other machine showed abnormal vibration (E11), maintenance history is clean (E10), and the sensor stream has no gaps around tick 71 (E3 samples every tick 55–80). A genuine mechanical fault (bearing, imbalance, mount, alignment) would be expected to coincide with elevated load, temperature rise, or persistent vibration — none of which is present. This points to a sensor/instrument disturbance (clipping, electrical interference, or injected value) rather than a machine health problem. Confidence is currently 0.80, below the 0.90 needed to authorize an intervention. One more check — CNC-03 vibration from tick 81 to 90 — would confirm sustained recovery and could raise confidence above the threshold; without it, the correct action is escalate rather than intervene.
